'''''Russelia equisetiformis''''', the '''fountainbush''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RUEQ|taxon=Russelia equisetiformis|accessdate=26 October 2015}}</ref> '''firecracker plant''', '''coral plant''', '''coral fountain''', '''coralblow''' or '''fountain plant''', is a species of flowering plant in the family  [[Plantaginaceae]].

This weeping [[subshrub]] is native to [[Mexico]] and [[Guatemala]].<ref name="smgrowers">[http://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=1403 San Marcos Growers horticultural database: ''Russelia equisetiformis''] . accessed 12.18.2013</ref>

The Latin [[specific epithet]] ''equisetiformis'' implies the plant has a form "like/similar to ''[[Equisetum]]''"—i.e., 'horsetail', 'horsetail rush/fern'—a genus  which ''Russelia'' is only distantly related to (and which is not a true [[fern]] genera).

==Description==
''Russelia equisetiformis'' is a multi-branching plant with thin leaves and arching foliage that measure around {{convert|4|-|5|ft|m}}.<ref name="smgrowers" /> The overall graceful form of the subshrub is a [[Habit (biology)|fountainesque]] mound. The stems and tiny oval leaves are bright green. It flowers profusely, with small, [[decumbent]] red flowers, earning the plant the common name 'firecracker fern' as it gives the impression of a bush set ablaze. It can bloom year-round in [[Tropics|tropical]] and [[Subtropics|subtropical]] [[Climate classification|climates]], such as [[Hardiness zone|USDA Hardiness zones]] 9-10, and above.<ref name="smgrowers"/>

''R. equisetiformis'' is favoured by [[nectar]]-feeding [[Anthecology|birds & insects]], due in-part to the trumpet-like, rather long flowers. Hummingbirds are especially drawn to ''Russelia''. 

==Cultivation==
''Russelia equisetiformis'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]], for [[Subtropics|subtropical]] & [[temperate climate|temperate]] gardens. In [[Tropics|tropical]] locations, it is recommended to be used as feature pots or hanging planters as it can become unruly in garden settings. Various colours exist ranging from white, yellow, pale orange & shades of red. Optimal conditions for flowering is a minimum of 4 hours of sunlight. The firecracker plant is capable of growing in a diverse range of settings, from desert to rain forest.

This species is best grown as a sprawling bordering or cascading groundcover where it accentuates its natural tufting rush-like habit.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ltd |first=GardensOnline Pty |title=Russelia equisetiformis {{!}} GardensOnline |url=https://www.gardensonline.com.au/gardenshed/plantfinder/show_1556.aspx |access-date=2023-09-08 |website=www.gardensonline.com.au}}</ref> It is equality suitable in a container (pot) as a feature. ''Russelia equisetiformis'' is especially attractive when grown in a basket, a hanging container, or otherwise cascading downwards, giving an appearance of cascading jungle cacti (like ''[[Hatiora]]'' or ''[[Rhipsalis]]'') or the thin-leaved ''[[Hoya (plant)|Hoya]]'' species ''[[Hoya linearis]]''. Once established, ''R. equisetiformis'' is moderately drought tolerant. In temperate climates, the  species is known to be semi-[[deciduous]]. The genus is reported to withstand temperatures down to {{convert|-6|C|F|abbr=on}}; still other authorities assert that it cannot tolerate temperatures below {{convert|5|C|F|abbr=on}}, nor can it handle frost, and therefore should be kept under glass or protected during the coldest months.<ref name="RHSPF" />  In colder climates, it can overwinter as a [[houseplant]] with access to direct sunlight or intense artificial lighting.<ref name="smgrowers" />

In the [[United Kingdom|UK]], ''Russelia equisetiformis'' has earned the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] (RHS)'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/16182/i-Russelia-equisetiformis-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - Russelia equisetiformis | accessdate = 11 October 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 93 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 11 October 2018}}</ref>
